prompt: You have now met four management orientations. Which philosophy is each company following?

cases.text: A car dealer has too many of last year's models, so it doubles sales commissions and runs promotions all weekend to move them.
cases.explanation: It follows an inside-out sequence starting from existing products and using heavy promotion to drive short-term sales volume.

cases.text: Before designing a stroller, a company spends months with city parents to identify the unmet problems they face on transit.
cases.explanation: It follows an outside-in sequence starting with a well-defined market and its underlying customer needs.

cases.text: A shoe manufacturer moves to a larger automated plant so it can lower unit costs and stock every discount store.
cases.explanation: Concentrating on production efficiency and broad distribution to keep offerings inexpensive and widely available is the production concept.

cases.text: An appliance maker focuses its budget on adding a faster motor and more engineering features to its blender every year.
cases.explanation: Focusing on continuous engineering improvements in quality, performance, and features is the product concept.

cases.text: A fitness club with unsold memberships hires a call center to phone every household in the district with high-pressure offers.
cases.explanation: It assumes consumers will not buy enough unless the firm undertakes a large-scale selling and promotional effort.

cases.text: A bank studies how university students manage rent and groceries, then coordinates an account, app, and support team around those needs.
cases.explanation: It identifies target market needs first and coordinates all marketing activities to earn profit through long-term satisfaction.

prompt: A restaurant chain is redesigning its operations under the societal marketing concept. Which of the three considerations does each requirement primarily address?

cards.text: Each new menu item must maintain a sustainable profit margin for the restaurant.
cards.explanation: The firm must generate company profits to remain viable.

cards.text: Meals must taste appealing and be ready within three minutes at the drive-through.
cards.explanation: Immediate taste and convenience satisfy short-run consumer wants.

cards.text: All single-use plastic wrappers and cups are replaced with certified compostable fiber.
cards.explanation: Eliminating persistent plastic waste protects society's long-run environmental welfare.

cards.text: The updated menu must sustain store-level revenue across all franchise locations.
cards.explanation: Store-level financial return supports company profits.

cards.text: Diners request indulgent late-night snack options at an affordable price.
cards.explanation: This reflects immediate individual consumer desires.

cards.text: Sodium and trans fats are reduced across the menu to lower long-term cardiovascular risk.
cards.explanation: Protecting long-term community health serves the long-run public interest.

prompt: Classify each situation as a human need, a culturally shaped want, or a market demand.

cards.text: Feeling cold and needing physical warmth during a January commute
cards.explanation: A state of felt deprivation representing a basic physical requirement for warmth and shelter.

cards.text: Experiencing a need for social belonging during the first week in a new city
cards.explanation: Belonging and affection are inherent social needs.

cards.text: Preferring a specific goose-down parka brand that peers on campus wear
cards.explanation: The underlying need for warmth takes a specific form shaped by culture and social context.

cards.text: Craving a bagel and specialty espresso on the morning train
cards.explanation: Hunger is the underlying need, while a bagel and espresso are culturally shaped wants.

cards.text: Having 1,200 dollars in savings ready to purchase a chosen laptop for coursework
cards.explanation: When a specific want is backed by financial buying power, it becomes a market demand.

cards.text: Paying for two commuter rail passes with a debit card at the station kiosk
cards.explanation: A want backed by purchasing power and willingness to pay is a demand.

prompt: Compare each buyer's prior expectations with the product's perceived performance. Is the buyer dissatisfied, satisfied, or delighted?

cards.text: A delivery app promises arrival in 30 minutes, but the meal arrives cold after an hour.
cards.explanation: Perceived performance fell below the buyer's prior expectations.

cards.text: A traveler books a standard room and receives a complimentary upgrade to a quiet corner suite.
cards.explanation: Perceived performance exceeded prior expectations, producing delight.

cards.text: A commuter buys a monthly transit pass expecting reliable daily trains, and every train runs on schedule.
cards.explanation: Perceived performance matched the buyer's prior expectations.

cards.text: Wireless earbuds advertised with an eight-hour battery lose charge after three hours of use.
cards.explanation: Performance fell short of the expectation set by the firm.

cards.text: A cloud storage plan promises automatic nightly backups, and files back up every night without issue.
cards.explanation: Performance matched what the customer expected.

cards.text: A repair shop quotes two days for a laptop fix, finishes it in three hours, and cleans the keyboard for free.
cards.explanation: Performance substantially exceeded the buyer's expectations.

prompt: Two founders launch a campus coffee roastery. Arrange their actions in the sequence of the five-step marketing process.

steps.text: Survey students and faculty to understand their morning routines, unmet needs, and price sensitivity.
steps.explanation: Step 1 is understanding the marketplace and customer needs and wants through research.

steps.text: Select commuter students as the target segment and promise ethically sourced coffee served in under 90 seconds.
steps.explanation: Step 2 is designing a customer-value-driven marketing strategy by selecting target customers and defining a value proposition.

steps.text: Develop the roast menu, set student pricing, lease a kiosk by the transit hub, and launch campus promotions.
steps.explanation: Step 3 is constructing an integrated marketing program across product, price, place, and promotion.

steps.text: Run a mobile loyalty community and respond to customer feedback to build lasting satisfaction and retention.
steps.explanation: Step 4 is engaging customers, building profitable relationships, and creating satisfaction and loyalty.

steps.text: Earn recurring semester sales, strong long-term profit margins, and growing customer equity.
steps.explanation: Step 5 is capturing value from customers in return through sales, profits, and customer equity.

prompt: Match each element of the integrated marketing mix (the Four Ps) with the corresponding managerial decision for a new commuter backpack.

pairs.match: Engineering a waterproof laptop compartment, ergonomic straps, protective packaging, and a lifetime repair warranty.
pairs.explanation: Product decisions encompass design, features, quality, packaging, and support services.

pairs.match: Setting a 110-dollar retail list price with a 15 percent student discount and three-month installment terms.
pairs.explanation: Price decisions cover list prices, discounts, and credit or payment terms.

pairs.match: Stocking the backpack in university bookstores, outdoor specialty retailers, and direct-to-consumer fulfillment warehouses.
pairs.explanation: Place (distribution) manages the channels that make the offering available and accessible to target buyers.

pairs.match: Running rain-test demonstration videos, campus ambassador reviews, and search ads explaining the warranty.
pairs.explanation: Promotion communicates the merits of the offering and persuades target customers to buy it.

question_text: A household that spends 150 dollars every week at a neighborhood grocery store switches permanently to a competitor after a five-dollar billing dispute is ignored. How does marketing analysis evaluate the retailer's loss?
hint: Distinguish a single transaction margin from Customer Lifetime Value (CLV).
correct_answer_citation: Week 1: Customer Lifetime Value and Share of Customer

options.option_text: The retailer loses only the five-dollar disputed amount from that transaction.
options.option_explanation: Focusing only on the immediate dispute ignores the future stream of purchases lost when the household defects.

options.option_text: The retailer loses the customer lifetime value representing tens of thousands of dollars in cumulative future purchases and margins.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Customer lifetime value (CLV) is the present value of the entire stream of purchases and profit margins generated over a lifetime of patronage.

options.option_text: The retailer's share of customer increases because fewer dissatisfied shoppers remain.
options.option_explanation: Share of customer is the portion of a buyer's category spending captured by the firm, which drops to zero when the household leaves.

options.option_text: The loss affects past market share metrics but has no effect on future customer equity.
options.option_explanation: Losing a household's future stream of purchases directly reduces future customer equity.

prompt: Classify each customer into one of the four relationship groups based on potential profitability and projected loyalty.

cases.text: A corporate consultant books expensive business-class suites but switches hotel chains whenever a rival runs a promotion.
cases.explanation: High potential profitability combined with low projected loyalty defines butterflies.

cases.text: A highway traveler buys a single pack of gum at a rural gas station and never passes through the region again.
cases.explanation: Low potential profitability and little projected loyalty define strangers.

cases.text: A household places high-margin weekly grocery and pharmacy orders with the same retailer for ten consecutive years.
cases.explanation: High potential profitability and high projected loyalty define true friends.

cases.text: An account holder keeps a 30-dollar minimum balance for decades while visiting the branch counter weekly for manual paper statements.
cases.explanation: High loyalty paired with revenue too low to cover the cost of service defines barnacles.

cases.text: A cycling enthusiast buys a premium road bike and annual maintenance package from the same local shop every two years.
cases.explanation: Both highly profitable and loyal, warranting continuous investment to nurture and retain.

cases.text: A bargain hunter buys only one deeply discounted clearance item per year and feels no attachment to the brand.
cases.explanation: Low profitability and little loyalty characterize strangers.
